en: I once vowed to take revenge.
If the Chinese flee in terror,
From the mouth of Keng-Jailak,
From the mountain of the golden mine,
I vowed to seize their land,
And avenge Almambet, Chubak, and Syrgak.
I vowed to settle their blood feud.
I will break through Beijing’s frontier
And proclaim, “This is Kyrgyz land,”
And raise up a khan.
After crushing the Khagan’s realm,
I intend, when Bakai has grown old,
To raise him as khan
Over the countless Chinese and their khagan.
Wheeling about and battling,
Shouting and thrusting spears,
When we turn upon the Khagan
I mean to bring him ruin.
When Kongurbay faces us,
If valiant Külchoro’s aim is true,
I mean to give him a spectacle.
The sands blaze and shimmer there;
If a cauldron is set upon the sand,
It roars and boils over.
No living creature
That encounters it survives.
Haze rises, gathering at the corners,
And dust billows through the hollows and ridges.
I will encircle the Chinese
And seize their land.
From the forty khans of teeming China
I mean to capture their armies.
From among Ulungtu’s sons,
From the mountains of Great Kaspan,
The perilous Kara-Suu—
This is the ill-fated place
Of which the ancients spoke.
From the plain of Kara-Suu,
From the mouth of Tash-Kapchal,
In the mountains of Kaspan-Tau,
There is a treasury of gold mines;
I intend to take its ore.
Kara-Tau, from which the forty Chinese tribes
Of Beijing obtain their tea—
That towering, lofty mountain—
I intend to take its land.
Wearing motley trousers and blue shirts,
Black caps and baggy breeches,
The many Chinese who look like women—
I intend to take their people.
Kara-Tau, where rubies are mined—
This place is called Kökhar-Sai.
I intend to seize
Their mules and camels as booty.
I intend to load up and carry away
The pure gold and white silver
Taken as booty from the Kakan.
I intend to smash his treasury,
Raze his city and take its gold coins,
Take its treasure as booty,
Load the gold coins upon the treasure,
And seize a thousand dark-eyed maidens.
My foe is Kakanchin;
I shall set my sights upon it,
Take it, and lay it waste.
Sary Khan’s bustling city—
I intend to lay it waste.
If I rage and exert my might,
Through the gorge where no people tread,
I shall make a road.
Beijing, beyond even the floodwaters’ reach—
My host shall reach it.
In Beijing, where no prophet has trodden,
When all the warriors stand together,
I believe my renown will reach its height.
The Khagan is the one I grapple with;
Kongurbay is the foe I have marked.
I mean to throw Beijing into turmoil,
And my heart is set
On capturing Kongurbay of Beijing.
We grew wrathful and stood defiant,
Ready to slaughter the Khagan’s people,
The black Kalmyks and the Manchus,
And strike them with a mighty blow.
Kongurbay is the one I grapple with,
To avenge my father.
Countless Chinese confront us;
We have firmly girded our waists
And set our faces toward Beijing
To pursue the blood-price of my fierce father
Manas.
I may well take pride in such
A kinsman as Külchoro,
Who closes with Kongurbay
And breaks his army.
Külchoro, my cherished support,
For such a cherished son
I would sacrifice my very life!
For God’s sake and for mine,
Go among the khans
Of the Khagan’s Chinese and return.
If your strength suffices, cast the Kalcha
Flat upon his back and bring him here.
If you are a warrior and a lion,
If you truly are brave Külchoro,
Strike straight at his blood;
If the Kalcha falls into your hands,
Capture him and bring him back alive!
My brave Külchoro, whom I cherish
As my support, go forth!
Though your fortune is full,
No lion like Koshoi will come from Talas;
My sheltering shadow whom I cherish,
No lion like you will arise among the Kyrgyz.
For a falcon-hearted son like you,
Your precious uncle would give his life!
Choros, for a son like you,
All the Kyrgyz together would give their lives!
You are the strength of my rugged back;
Since fierce Manas passed away,
No kinsman has remained to support me.
Merely seeing you puts my heart at rest;
There is no refuge against death,
Yet whenever I see you my heart is at peace.
I have no other shadow in this world but you.
Cursed be loneliness!
My heart burns, and my liver is embers.
Whenever I think, “May my fierce
Külchoro, my cherished support, live safely,”
My heart is comforted.
There is no steed to mount for battle,
To enter the foe with cunning
And charge them with a shout.
Your lonely uncle grieves,
For he has no kinsman but you alone.
Praying that the Creator sustain you,
He goes alone as envoy.
Upon poor Külchoro
May the Creator turn His gaze;
He has no steed to ride on patrol.
Father Creator, do not leave him desolate:
He has no kinsman but this Choro.
I have no stalwart back to bear my mark,
No people but this Choro.”
So Semetey spoke:
“China is a vast realm and the hero is alone—
God, protect my Choro!
Father, for a son like Külchoro
May the roaring Kyrgyz and the many Argyn
All give themselves in sacrifice!”
The people heeded Semetey’s words;
The countless Kyrgyz and many Argyn
Grieved with him, crying aloud.
Khan Bakai raised his hands,
While elsewhere men sobbed and wailed.
The multitude of Kyrgyz wept,
And all the khan’s giants wept.
“Whenever battle calls, this lone hero
Enters against whatever foe he chooses,
With no one at all to support him.
Whenever the hour comes, this gray wolf
Goes in all alone.
If my destined end comes, I shall die;
But for this dear Choro of mine,
Someday, at some hour,
What can I, poor father’s only son,
Possibly do?”
The fierce lion grieved,
Then angrily set about his task,
His heart aflame with embers.
The splendid, noble hero
Would slaughter the Kaldai and settle the blood-price;
Wondering what would become of his Choro,
The valiant man’s heart smoked with anguish.
Father, noble lion, proud as a cock,
Your warrior stands close to greatness;
He is truly a gray-wolf hero.
Your lion-born hero by descent,
Your lion Choro, Almambet’s son,
Your openhearted warrior Choro,
Slung on his jezail,
And, his heart burning, the noble hero
Pleaded with his uncle:
“Do not grieve every day
Over your doomed son, my khan and uncle.
Between infidel and Muslim,
Such is the way of holy war;
Who could be pleased by it?
Father, do not keep grieving, khan and uncle,
Over your luckless servant.
If I remain alive and do not die,
I am a son worth a sheepskin;
If I fall and lie stretched dead,
I am a slave-son worth a dogskin.
You have firmly girded your waist,
But why should you grieve so bitterly,
As though this valiant man were born beside you,
Or sprang from the very loins
Of moonlike Manas,
Or tore his way from the womb
Of my dark-faced mother Kanykei?
Why stand there mourning?
My sorrowing warrior-uncle,
Do not grieve and torment yourself:
Where was I ever Manas’s son?
Warrior, silver-eyed and sun-faced,
My thundering lion of an uncle,
Who brought the whole world under his sway,
Father, my beloved heroic uncle,
Kongurbay is the one I truly contend with.
I have thoroughly deceived the swine;
If the chance comes, I shall cut him down.
Ezkara is the one I stalk;
If the Kalmyk gives me an opening,
I shall overturn and fling him aside.
I shall beat the calculated fury from him.
Kongurbay is the enemy I stalk;
I have deceived your dog
And shall somehow find a way.
Father, my beloved uncle,
If my appointed death comes, I shall die.
If death has not come and my days are not done,
If my skill suffices, I shall make
A wondrous spectacle of the Kalcha.
You were both guileless and lionhearted;
You had courage but no caution,
A fierce hero who would heed no counsel.
Understand what I tell you;
My magnanimous uncle, heed my words.
Understand what I am saying;
Uncle of my dark day, heed my words!
I shall make my valor known.
Alööke’s Kongurbay
Has a black horse, that infidel’s mount,
With wings upon its flanks;
Wherever ear has heard or eye has seen,
It races in a frenzy across the earth—
Such has ever been its way.
I shall make my heroism known
And bring that black horse into our hands.
The forty tribes of China are a mighty realm,
A host as countless as black worms.
Do not let the Chinese recover;
Even if they bow like brides,
Do not let them trick you out of the black horse again.
They have marksmen and hosts like floods;
If they engulf us in their wrath,
Remember that ever since your father Manas,
Kongurbay has always
Made deceit his way.
I pretended to be Chinese
And practiced deceit beyond all measure.
Thus shall I bring the haughty Kalcha
Into our hands.
My valiant, lionhearted uncle,
When you confront him, strike hard;
